item.message: `[features].memory_tool` is deprecated. Use `[features].memories` instead. (Enable it with `--enable memories` or `[features].memories` in config.toml. See https://developers.openai.com/codex/config-basic#feature-flags for details.)

item.text:
1. **Section 2(1)(A) — Undefined “artificial intelligence model.”** The bill never distinguishes a model from related software, an ensemble, a collection of specialized models, or a larger system incorporating a model. That uncertainty permits architectures to be characterized as multiple sub-threshold models rather than one covered model.

2. **Section 2(1)(A) — Undefined “trained.”** It is unclear whether “trained” includes pretraining, post-training, fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, distillation, continual learning, retrieval-index construction, or updates made through user interaction. Work characterized as development, adaptation, or inference-time optimization may therefore fall outside the compute test.

3. **Section 2(1)(A) — Undefined “single training run.”** The bill supplies no rule for deciding when a run begins or ends, or whether checkpoints, restarts, phased training, distributed jobs, and successive fine-tunes are one run. A project could potentially divide training into nominally separate runs, each below the threshold.

4. **Section 2(1)(A) — No aggregation across related models or runs.** Compute used in experiments, failed runs, hyperparameter searches, precursor models, distillation, and successive versions is not expressly aggregated. The threshold apparently applies only to the compute used for the particular model in one particular run.

5. **Section 2(1)(A) — Strict “greater than” threshold.** A model trained using exactly \(10^{26}\) operations is not covered by paragraph (A). Measurement error around the threshold could also make coverage indeterminate.

6. **Section 2(1)(A) — Undefined operation-counting methodology.** The text does not say whether to count theoretical or executed operations, forward and backward passes, sparse operations, recomputation, data processing, communication, or work performed by non-chip hardware. Different reasonable accounting methods could produce different legal outcomes.

7. **Section 2(1)(A) — Technology-specific metric.** Only “integer or floating-point operations” are counted, leaving uncertainty about analog, neuromorphic, optical, quantum, lookup-based, or other computation not conventionally recorded as integer or floating-point operations.

8. **Section 2(1)(A) — No measurement, recordkeeping, or certification mechanism.** The bill does not require model developers to measure or preserve training-compute records and gives the government no prescribed method for proving the threshold was exceeded.

9. **Section 2(1)(B) — Undefined “artificial intelligence system.”** This term may be broader than the “model” referenced in paragraph (A), but the relationship between the two is never explained. Coverage may change depending on whether capabilities are attributed to the underlying model, surrounding tools, retrieval systems, or the complete product.

10. **Section 2(1)(B) — Unidentified Secretary.** “The Secretary” is not defined. Although Commerce may be inferred from section 4, the statute does not expressly identify the official empowered to make capability determinations.

11. **Section 2(1)(B) — No procedure for capability determinations.** The bill specifies no testing process, evidentiary standard, notice, hearing, publication, appeal, effective date, or requirement that a determination identify a particular system version. It is consequently unclear when a system becomes covered and whether a determination can operate retroactively.

12. **Section 2(1)(B) — Vague capability standard.** “Capable of substantially exceeding human performance across most cognitive tasks” does not define “capable,” “substantially,” “human performance,” “most,” or “cognitive tasks.” Coverage could depend on which humans, tasks, metrics, prompting, tools, time limits, and operating conditions are selected.

13. **Section 2(1)(B) — Latent versus demonstrated capability.** The bill does not say whether a system is “capable” when the capability is theoretically possible, elicited only with special scaffolding, or demonstrated in ordinary deployment. This makes pre-deployment compliance determinations especially difficult.

14. **Section 2(1)(B) — No treatment of changing systems.** A system’s capabilities may change through tools, data access, software updates, or deployment context without additional training. The bill does not state whether a prior determination follows every copy and configuration or must be renewed.

15. **Section 2(2) — Underinclusive definition of “U.S. person.”** The definition includes only U.S. citizens and corporations organized under state law. It omits permanent residents, nationals who are not citizens, partnerships, trusts, associations, LLCs not treated as corporations, and potentially entities organized under federal, District of Columbia, territorial, or tribal law.

16. **Section 2(2) — Foreign subsidiaries and affiliates.** A separately incorporated foreign subsidiary is not a “U.S. person” merely because it has a U.S. parent. Work conducted abroad by such an entity may escape subsection 3(a) unless the parent itself can be shown to have trained, developed, or deployed the system.

17. **Sections 2(2) and 3(a) — “Person” is not expressly defined.** The general Dictionary Act may supply a definition, but the relationship between that general term and the unusually narrow bespoke definition of “U.S. person” is unclear, particularly for entities and government bodies.

18. **Section 2(3) — Undefined “data center.”** The bill provides no rule for identifying the boundaries of a data center. A campus could potentially be divided into separate buildings, suites, operators, or nominal facilities, each below the threshold.

19. **Section 2(3) — Undefined “advanced AI chips.”** No performance, interconnect, age, export-control classification, or intended-use criterion identifies which chips count. Commodity accelerators, custom ASICs, older GPUs, and nontraditional accelerators therefore have uncertain status.

20. **Section 2(3) — Strict chip-count threshold.** A facility containing exactly 50,000 qualifying chips is not covered because the definition requires “more than” 50,000. The rule also encourages distributing compute among several facilities.

21. **Section 2(3) — Ambiguous “containing.”** It is unclear whether chips in storage, under repair, disconnected, leased to customers, in transit, or not available for a common workload count. The definition also does not address virtual or remote pooling of chips across locations.

22. **Section 2(3) — Facility status can fluctuate.** No measurement date or averaging period is provided. A facility could move above and below the threshold, leaving unclear when registration attaches or whether deregistration is possible.

23. **Section 3(a) — Undefined prohibited acts.** “Train,” “develop,” and “deploy” have no statutory definitions. The text does not clearly prohibit possession, use, operation, access, importation, sale, licensing, financing, publication, maintenance, or assistance by a party that did not itself perform one of the three named acts.

24. **Section 3(a) — No express prohibition on attempts or facilitation.** The bill does not itself prohibit attempting, conspiring to, aiding, or causing another person to train, develop, or deploy a covered system. Other generally applicable criminal doctrines may sometimes apply, but their reach would not be coextensive with a direct statutory prohibition.

25. **Section 3(a) — Offshore work by non-U.S. persons.** Foreign persons operating outside the United States are beyond the provision’s stated territorial and nationality coverage. The bill does not prohibit U.S. persons from purchasing access to a foreign-developed system unless that conduct itself constitutes “deploying” it.

26. **Section 3(a) — Territorial ambiguity for online activity.** The text does not explain when cloud-based or distributed conduct occurs “in the United States”—for example, where the user, developer, corporate decision-maker, server, or model is located.

27. **Section 3(a) — No treatment of open publication.** Publishing model weights, source code, or training methods is not expressly listed. Whether publication constitutes “develop” or “deploy” is uncertain and could also raise First Amendment questions.

28. **Sections 2(1)(A) and 3(a) — Coverage may arise only after the threshold is crossed.** A model is not covered under paragraph 2(1)(A) until it has been trained using more than the threshold amount, creating uncertainty about the exact point at which otherwise lawful training becomes prohibited and whether the threshold-crossing operation itself is a violation.

29. **Section 3(b) — Minimal pre-enactment work may secure grandfathering.** The exception turns solely on whether “training began” before enactment and supplies no minimum duration, compute expenditure, or good-faith-development requirement. A token training step before enactment could plausibly be asserted to grandfather a system.

30. **Section 3(b) — Grandfathering has no limit on later training.** The exception does not say that only pre-enactment training is protected or impose a cap on post-enactment scaling, fine-tuning, or continual learning. Once training has begun, the text can be read to exempt the system from subsection 3(a) altogether.

31. **Section 3(b) — Exception covers development and deployment, not just training.** Because subsection 3(b) says subsection 3(a) “shall not apply” to the grandfathered system, it apparently permits its indefinite post-enactment development and deployment, rather than merely allowing completion of an existing training run.

32. **Section 3(b) — No rule for successor systems.** The bill does not specify whether a fine-tuned model, merged model, checkpoint, derivative, distilled version, or substantially redesigned descendant is the same grandfathered “system.” Developers could argue that later versions retain the original system’s pre-enactment training history.

33. **Section 3(b) — Capability-based systems may have no clear training start.** Systems covered under paragraph 2(1)(B) may consist of multiple existing components or may acquire capabilities through tooling rather than a discrete training run. It may be impossible to determine when “training began” for purposes of the exception.

34. **Section 3(c) — Unrestricted safety-evaluation exception.** “Activities conducted for the purpose of safety evaluation” is undefined and requires no approval, protocol, independent supervision, reporting, duration limit, or containment. Training, development, and even deployment could be characterized as necessary to evaluate safety.

35. **Section 3(c) — Mixed-purpose activities.** The bill does not require safety evaluation to be the sole or primary purpose. An activity with simultaneous commercial, research, and safety purposes may therefore qualify.

36. **Section 3(c) — No restriction on who conducts evaluations.** Any actor can apparently invoke the exception; it is not limited to government agencies, accredited laboratories, or independent evaluators. Nor does the bill limit the scale or number of copies created for evaluation.

37. **Section 4(a) — Undefined “operator.”** Ownership, physical control, leasing, colocation management, and workload scheduling may reside in different entities. The bill does not identify which one must register or allocate responsibility among multiple operators.

38. **Section 4(a) — No registration deadline or required content.** The statute does not say when registration must occur, what information must be submitted, when an amended registration is required, or whether Commerce must create a registry before the duty attaches.

39. **Section 4(a) — Possible extraterritorial registry.** “Each covered facility” is not limited to facilities in the United States or facilities operated by U.S. persons. Read literally, it purports to register every qualifying facility worldwide, while providing no clear jurisdictional basis or mechanism for doing so.

40. **Section 4(b) — Indeterminate quarterly reporting obligation.** The reporting period, due date, format, level of detail, treatment of customer-confidential data, and meaning of “describing” workloads are unspecified. A high-level description may technically satisfy the text.

41. **Section 4(b) — Ambiguous certification.** “Certified by the operator” does not state what facts are being certified, under what standard of knowledge, or by which individual when the operator is an entity. There is no express attestation language or audit requirement.

42. **Sections 4 and 5 — Registry violations have no specified penalty.** Section 5 penalizes only violations of section 3. Failure to register, report, report on time, or provide an accurate report therefore carries no penalty under this Act, although other generally applicable laws could apply to knowingly false submissions.

43. **Section 4 — No relation between facilities and the substantive prohibition.** Section 3 applies regardless of facility size, while section 4 addresses only facilities with more than 50,000 chips. Major training could be distributed among smaller unregistered facilities, and registration itself neither authorizes nor prohibits any workload.

44. **Section 5(a) — Conflict with the effective date.** Civil penalties purport to cover violations “occurring on or after” enactment, but section 8 says the Act does not take effect until 180 days later. Conduct during that interval cannot readily violate a prohibition not yet in effect, making the penalty language internally inconsistent.

45. **Section 5(a) — Unclear calculation of daily violations.** The bill does not say whether each model, prohibited act, facility, or responsible person creates a separate violation, or when a violation begins and ends. An instantaneous training or deployment act also fits awkwardly with a per-day penalty.

46. **Section 5(a) — No civil enforcement machinery.** The Act does not identify the enforcing department, authorize an administrative proceeding or civil action, specify a limitations period, provide subpoena or inspection authority, or establish factors for selecting a penalty up to $1 million.

47. **Section 5(b) — Ambiguous “willfully” standard.** The bill does not say whether the government must prove knowledge of the facts, knowledge that the system was legally covered, or knowledge that the conduct was unlawful. The vagueness of the coverage standards would compound that uncertainty.

48. **Section 5(b) — No offense-specific procedural provisions.** The provision supplies no venue rule, limitations period, forfeiture authority, treatment of continuing offenses, or express rules for corporate and individual responsibility. General federal law may fill some gaps but not necessarily all of them.

49. **Sections 2–5 — No designated administering agency.** Commerce receives registrations, but no agency is expressly charged with interpreting or enforcing the prohibition, making capability determinations, conducting audits, or issuing compliance guidance.

50. **Sections 2–5 — No rulemaking authority.** The bill contains no express authority or deadline to define its central technical terms, establish compute-accounting standards, create reporting forms, or update the chip and compute thresholds as technology changes.

51. **Sections 2(1)(B), 3, and 5 — Fair-notice and delegation concerns.** Criminal liability may depend on an unidentified Secretary’s application of highly subjective terms without statutory procedures or intelligible technical criteria. That invites due-process vagueness and nondelegation challenges, especially where a determination is unpublished or postdates the conduct.

52. **Section 6 — International provision is aspirational only.** The Secretary of State need only “seek to negotiate”; there is no requirement to conclude, submit, implement, or enforce an agreement. Failure to obtain foreign participation has no effect on the domestic prohibition.

53. **Section 7(a) — No required National Academies report.** Termination depends on Congress “acting on” a National Academies report, but the Act neither commissions such a report nor sets a deadline, scope, funding source, or procedure for producing one.

54. **Section 7(a) — Undefined “acting on” and safety finding.** The provision does not explain what connection the joint resolution must have to the report or what evidence supports a finding that systems “can be developed safely.” It also does not specify the language or effective date of the terminating resolution.

55. **Section 7(a) — Termination affects only section 3.** If Congress makes the specified finding before the ten-year sunset, only “the prohibition in section 3” ends; the facility registration and reporting regime apparently continues until section 7(b) terminates the entire Act.

56. **Sections 7(a) and 7(b) — Competing duration provisions.** Section 7(a) says the prohibition remains until Congress makes a finding, while section 7(b) ends the entire Act after ten years regardless of any finding. The sunset likely controls, but the two provisions are not harmonized expressly.

57. **Section 7(b) — Abrupt sunset of all obligations and liabilities.** The Act does not preserve pending enforcement actions, accrued penalties, records, or prosecutions after the ten-year sunset. The absence of a specific savings clause could generate disputes about whether pre-sunset liabilities survive, notwithstanding the general federal saving statute.

58. **Section 8 — No transition rules.** The 180-day delay does not address systems begun after enactment but before effectiveness, pending Secretary determinations, registration preparation, or conduct continuing across the effective date. In particular, such systems are lawful during the delay yet do not literally qualify for section 3(b)’s pre-enactment grandfathering.

59. **Act-wide — No severability clause.** If a court invalidates the discretionary capability test, criminal application, or another central provision, the Act gives no direction on whether the remaining provisions should stand. Ordinary severability doctrine would apply, but the outcome would be uncertain.

60. **Act-wide — No appropriations or implementation resources.** The Act mandates registration, reporting, capability determinations, enforcement, and international negotiations without authorizing funding or staffing. That may not invalidate the duties, but it makes timely and consistent implementation doubtful.
